newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin's pneumonia fuels talk of power struggles.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin's pneumonia fuels talk of power struggles.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin's admission to hospital with pneumonia fuelled speculation on Thursday that political rivals, scenting the chance of an early election, will start a new round of in-fighting and power struggles.

During Yeltsin's almost six-month absence from the Kremlin with heart problems last year, some officials traded open insults and others manoeuvred for position behind the scenes in the belief that the president might never come back.

Yeltsin, 65, managed to limit the damage by sacking one of the major players, his national security adviser Alexander Lebed, in October and defied the odds by making a triumphant return to the Kremlin on December 23.
The danger now is that, if his new setback proves lasting, the cracks which he has papered over will reopen, carrying the risk of political instablity.
"There's simply a power vacuum. There's no power in the country. It's rudderless," Lebed told reporters on Thursday, following Yeltsin's admission to hospital on Wednesday night.
The former paratroop commander left no doubt who he believed should fill that vacuum and lost no time in attacking one of his rivals for power, Kremlin chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais.

"The question of the president's departure over his health is on the agenda. The longer this rule by a regent (Chubais), the graver the consequences," said Lebed, who accused Chubais of usurping power while Yeltsin was absent with heart trouble.
Doctors have not said how long the president will be out of the Kremlin this time. But the longer he is away, the greater the chances are that the battles for influence will resume.

The manoeuvres by Lebed and his rivals over the summer, as Yeltsin prepared for heart surgery on November 5, deepened divisions in the Kremlin and threatened Russia's stability until Yeltsin sacked Lebed.

Lebed appeared at the time to have erred in the belief that the president would be unable to serve out his four-year term, due to end in the middle of the year 2000, and that an early election would be called.
But political analysts said Yeltsin's latest illness could give Lebed and other would-be presidents new hope that the Kremlin leader will be forced to bow out early.

"Even if this disease is not very serious, it increases the political instability in this country," Andrei Piontowski, head of Moscow's Centre for Strategic Studies think tank, told the British Broadcasting Corporation.
"We are returning to the situation of October and November when there was a real presidential race between the would-be candidates."
Lebed, 46, was third in last year's presidential election and has retained wide popularity, although his blunt talk makes him a loose cannon the West finds hard to trust.
Many political experts say his chances of victory would be particularly good if an election were called soon.

Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, 58, is the likely choice of the political and big business establishment. But he appears to have little voter appeal, especially as the government has failed to pay some workers for several months.
Moscow Mayor Yuri Luzhkov, 60, is another Yeltsin ally who looks likely to run in the next election, scheduled for the year 2000. But his popularity appears limited to the capital.
All these candidates need time to develop their image and mount a campaign.

Opposition Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov, 52, who finished second to Yeltsin in last year's election, has already spent much time preparing a new bid. But critics say the communists have little chance after last summer's defeat.

Some political analysts say Russia has proved it can maintain a measure of stability without Yeltsin in the Kremlin. But if in-fighting increases, there will be a greater risk of instablility finally getting out of hand.
"Last year showed Yeltsin's absence caused stagnation and power struggles. The whole thing will become serious if Yeltsin is ill for a longer time," a European diplomat said.
